title: New Materialism and Haraway
keyWorks: J. Bennett, The Enchantment of Modern Life (2001)
D. Haraway, The Companion Species Manifesto (2003)
D. Haraway, Staying with the Trouble (2016)
summary: New materialism is a current of philosophy from the 2000s and 2010s that invites us to look at matter afresh: not as passive raw material but as something lively, active, capable of making a difference. Jane Bennett speaks of "vibrant matter" and "thing-power", while Donna Haraway, who is close to this current, writes about our kinship with other species and about the need to "stay with the trouble" of our time, fleeing neither into despair nor into faith in a miraculous rescue.
onEmotions: For new materialism, feelings are not purely inner, "spiritual" events. They arise in assemblages (Bennett borrows the term from Deleuze) made of the body, food, weather, things, other people and creatures. This lifts part of the load from you: your mood is not only your "achievement" or your "fault". Bennett especially values "enchantment" — a sense of wonder at the world which, she believes, nourishes ethical generosity. Haraway stresses that the hard feelings of our time are better lived through together, in kinship with others, by cultivating "response-ability" — the capacity to respond.

anxiety.text: Anxiety today is often tied to a feeling that the world is falling apart and the future is closed. In Staying with the Trouble, Donna Haraway offers a particular way of living with this feeling. She criticises two familiar reactions: the belief that technology or someone else will save us, and the weary "there's nothing to be done anymore". Both, for Haraway, lead us away from the present. Instead she proposes "staying with the trouble" — being here, in a tangled, unsettled world, together with other beings, doing what is possible. Seen this way, anxiety needs neither to be inflated into the end of the world nor to be silenced. You can bring it back into the present: notice that you are already here, among the living, and that there is a small thing that makes sense right now.
anxiety.practice: Name one small thing that makes sense to do today — for yourself, for someone near you, or for the place where you live.

quote.text: Staying with the trouble requires learning to be truly present, not as a vanishing pivot between awful or edenic pasts and apocalyptic or salvific futures, but as mortal critters entwined in myriad unfinished configurations of places, times, matters, meanings.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

fear.text: Fear often makes us shrink and wall ourselves off. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett shows that the world is full of forces that don't obey our control: power grids, food, weather, even trash have what she calls "thing-power". We are not the only ones who act; action is distributed among many participants. This might sound unsettling, but there is relief in it too. From the new materialist point of view, you don't have to hold the whole world under control on your own — that is impossible for anyone. You can acknowledge fear as the normal reaction of a creature among many forces. And then ask yourself: which of these forces are holding me up? Things can be a support as well — a warm blanket, a cup of tea, the ground under your feet.
fear.practice: Find three things around you that are supporting you right now — literally, physically. Touch each one and name it.

quote.text: The capacity of things — edibles, commodities, storms, metals — not only to impede or block the will and designs of humans but also to act as quasi agents or forces with trajectories, propensities, or tendencies of their own.
quote.author: Jane Bennett

sadness.text: Sadness is usually thought of as something purely inner — "in my soul". New materialism suggests widening the view. Jane Bennett writes that a human being is an "assemblage", made of many elements: the body, bacteria, food, light, things and relationships. She discusses, for example, how what we eat can affect mood — as if matter itself takes part in our feelings. Seen this way, sadness is not proof of your failure but the state of a whole assemblage you are part of: a lack of sunlight, a tired body, a loss, the weather may all be involved. This doesn't diminish the feeling; it makes it more understandable and gentler. And it offers a hint: sometimes the assemblage can be shifted a little very simply — by stepping into the light or spending time near something alive.
sadness.practice: List what is part of your "assemblage" right now: weather, sleep, food, people, place. Is there one element that would be easy to change a little?

grief.text: Grief is love's answer to loss, and it deserves room. Donna Haraway writes a great deal about mourning in an age of vanishing species and insists that grieving is important work, not weakness. Following the philosopher Thom van Dooren, she says that mourning helps us understand how deeply we are entangled with others. For Haraway, what has gone does not vanish without a trace: in her images, all living things "compost" one another, passing on matter, stories and connections. She even says that "we are compost, not posthuman". Seen this way, your grief is part of a long thread that binds you to what you have lost, and through it to the living. You can let mourning be shared and slow, without hurrying to "finish" it alone.
grief.practice: Think of someone with whom you could share one memory of what you have lost. Just name that person.

loneliness.text: Loneliness tells you that you are missing connection — and that is an important truth. Donna Haraway offers a bold idea: kinship doesn't have to be only by blood. In Staying with the Trouble she calls on us to "make kin" — with friends, neighbours, a chosen family, and also with animals, plants and places. Earlier, in The Companion Species Manifesto, she described how people and dogs have shaped each other over centuries. Seen this way, loneliness is not a final state but an invitation to new connections, sometimes unusual ones. Kinship can be not only received but woven: from a regular walk, from caring for a plant, from a short conversation with someone you see every day.
loneliness.practice: Name one creature, place or person with whom a small "kinship" could begin. What first gesture of attention is possible?

quote.text: We become-with each other or not at all.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

anger.text: Anger often arises when we see injustice, and it is a legitimate reaction. Donna Haraway doesn't ask us to suppress it: she herself writes sharply about the destruction of habitats and about those who pay for it. But she offers a particular turn — towards "response-ability". It's a play on words: responsibility, and the ability to respond. For Haraway, what matters is not only naming the guilty but learning to respond: what can I do, whom can I join, whom can I care for? Seen this way, anger can be respected as energy and directed into a response. This doesn't cancel the anger but makes it fruitful: it stops burning you from within and becomes a bond with those you want to protect.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: what or whom do I want to respond to with this anger? Write down one possible act of response — any one, however small.

shame.text: Shame often rests on the idea that you must be a whole, separate, flawless "self". New materialism gently takes this image apart. Jane Bennett shows that a person is an assemblage, made of many elements, many of which are beyond your control: bacteria, hormones, environment, the things around you. Back in A Cyborg Manifesto, Donna Haraway wrote that we are all hybrids, mixtures of the organic and the technical, the natural and the cultural — and she saw in this not a flaw but a possibility. Seen this way, the ideal of a person in full control of themselves is a fantasy. You don't have to answer for every movement of your feelings and body as if you were their sole master. This doesn't cancel responsibility, but it can loosen shame's grip: you are a living tangle, not a statue.
shame.practice: Recall what you feel ashamed of and ask: what forces, besides my will, took part in this situation? Name at least two.

guilt.text: Guilt shows that the consequences of your actions matter to you. Jane Bennett suggests seeing action as distributed: almost any event — from a power outage to an illness — happens through an assemblage of many participants, human and non-human. In Vibrant Matter she examines a major blackout in the power grid that had no single culprit. Seen this way, the guilt you carry entirely on your own shoulders is often actually shared among many forces. Bennett doesn't release people from responsibility, but she invites us to see it more modestly and precisely: you are one of the participants, not the sole author. This understanding helps you move from self-punishment to the question: which part of this is mine to change?
guilt.practice: Draw the situation as a diagram with several participants — people, circumstances, things. Circle only your own part.

envy.text: Envy is often born of a picture of life as a competition between separate individuals: who has more, who is more successful. Donna Haraway offers a different picture. She speaks of "sympoiesis" — "making-with": nothing living makes itself; everything comes about together with others, in entanglements. Her favourite image is the string-figure game, cat's cradle, where the pattern is formed by the hands of many players passing the string to one another. Seen this way, someone else's success is also a pattern woven by many hands, not a personal victory over you. Envy doesn't disappear, but it softens. You can ask yourself: which patterns am I part of? Where is my thread already holding something important?
envy.practice: Name one shared project, relationship or community where your "thread" is holding something. What would be different without you?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can feel as though the world has lost its colour. In The Enchantment of Modern Life, Jane Bennett argues with Max Weber's famous idea of the "disenchantment of the world" — the notion that modernity is stripped of mystery and wonder. She shows that enchantment — surprise, a slight shock at the extraordinary within the ordinary — is still possible: in nature, in the city, in words, even in technology. Bennett believes this feeling is not a luxury but a source of energy from which generosity and care for others grow. Seen this way, emptiness doesn't need to be filled right away with grand meanings. You can begin with the smallest encounter with matter — a smell, a texture, a sound — which gently reminds you that the world is still alive.
emptiness.practice: Choose one sensation right now — the touch of fabric, a sound outside the window, the taste of water — and stay with it for thirty seconds.

confusion.text: Confusion arises when familiar divisions — living and non-living, self and world, nature and culture — stop working. New materialism openly admits that these boundaries really are porous. The physicist and philosopher Karen Barad speaks of "intra-action": things don't first exist separately; they take shape through their interaction. Donna Haraway proposes "tentacular thinking" — thinking not in straight lines but in curves, like a creature with tentacles feeling its way through the world. Seen this way, confusion is not a failure but a possible beginning of such thinking. When you don't know where the boundaries lie, you may be closer to reality than someone who is sure of everything. You can let yourself feel your way through the situation little by little, without demanding a clear map right away.
confusion.practice: Instead of looking for the whole answer, ask one "tentacular" question: what can I learn about this situation in the next hour?

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are a signal that the body can no longer keep up the pace it has been given. New materialism suggests treating the body as a full participant, not as a tool commanded by the will. Jane Bennett writes about "thing-power" — the capacity of matter to resist, to dig in its heels, to act in its own way. Following Spinoza, she speaks of "conatus" — the striving of every body to preserve itself. Seen this way, your exhaustion is the voice of the matter you are made of, and it deserves respect, not to be overcome. Your body, too, needs to preserve itself. Rest, then, is not laziness or weakness of will but cooperation with your own matter: you listen to it rather than argue with it.
fatigue.practice: Ask your body — your shoulders, your back, your eyes: what do you need right now? Do at least a small part of it.

boredom.text: Boredom appears when the world seems flat and predictable. Jane Bennett offers an antidote — "enchantment". For her it isn't fairy-tale magic but an entirely real feeling: a brief moment of stillness when something extraordinary suddenly shows through the familiar. Bennett believes enchantment can be cultivated — by slowing down, looking closely, allowing yourself to be surprised. In Vibrant Matter she recalls how she once noticed a chance gathering of things on a storm drain grate — a work glove, pollen, a bottle cap, a stick — and they suddenly seemed to her shimmering and alive. Seen this way, boredom is not a property of the world but a tiredness of the eye. You can give the world a chance to surprise you.
boredom.practice: Find a chance gathering of small things near you — on your desk, on the windowsill — and describe it as if it were an archaeologist's find.

quote.text: To be enchanted is to be struck and shaken by the extraordinary that lives amid the familiar and the everyday.
quote.author: Jane Bennett

joy.text: For new materialism, joy is not just a pleasant state but an important force. Jane Bennett argues that the joy of encountering the world — enchantment — nourishes ethics: to care for the world, you need at least sometimes to delight in it. Without this, she believes, moral demands turn into a heavy duty. Donna Haraway, for her part, writes with humour and playfulness even about the most serious things and calls her work a game of string figures. Seen this way, joy is not frivolity against a backdrop of trouble but fuel for care. You can let yourself rejoice without holding back — in an animal nearby, a patch of sunlight on the floor, the taste of an apple — and know that this joy makes you a more alive participant in the shared world.
joy.practice: Name one thing or one creature that made you glad today, and recall that moment in every detail.

love.text: Love and tenderness are central themes for Donna Haraway. In The Companion Species Manifesto she writes about her dog, her partner in agility training, and shows that love between species is not sentimentality but serious, bodily, sometimes difficult work of mutual learning. For Haraway, to love is to "become-with": you change alongside another, and they change alongside you. No one stays the same. Seen this way, tenderness is not a fixed state but a shared process that requires attention to who the other really is, not who you imagine them to be. This helps you accept the hard sides of love too — the mismatches, the adjusting to each other, the work. All of this is part of becoming together.
love.practice: Recall what you have learned from someone you love — a person or an animal. Name one change in yourself.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is the recognition that you did not make yourself. New materialism shows how literally true this is. Donna Haraway speaks of "sympoiesis" — making-with: living things are made together, in webs of interdependence, from the bacteria in your gut to the people who raised you. Jane Bennett adds that things take part in our lives too: bread, water, sunlight are not passive resources but co-participants. Seen this way, gratitude is not only politeness towards people but attention to the whole assemblage that supports you. You can silently thank the chair that holds you and the water you drink — not in a magical sense, but as a way of noticing that you are woven into a living world.
gratitude.practice: List five non-human "co-participants" in your day today — from coffee to sunlight.

hope.text: For Donna Haraway, hope is not the belief that everything will sort itself out. In Staying with the Trouble she criticises both technological optimism and apocalyptic despair. She proposes the notion of the "Chthulucene" — named after the spider Pimoa cthulhu and the Greek word "chthonic", meaning of the earth, underground. This is her name for a time in which humans and other beings learn to live and recover together, amid damaged places. Hope here is modest and practical: in small communities, in restoration projects, in stories about surviving together. Haraway especially values stories, because they shape which worlds we will be able to build. Seen this way, to hope is to choose and tell stories that have room for a future.
hope.practice: Recall one real story about something damaged that recovered thanks to care. Tell it to yourself again.

quote.text: It matters what stories make worlds, what worlds make stories.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a longing for the past, for places and things that are no longer what they were. New materialism treats it with understanding, because it takes things and places seriously. Jane Bennett shows that objects are not passive carriers of memory but participants in our lives: an old mug, the smell of a home, a particular street really do affect us. Seen this way, nostalgia is not just "a memory in your head" but a response to a real connection with the material world that has changed. In Donna Haraway's spirit, one could add that the past doesn't leave entirely: it goes on living in matter, in bodies, in stories. You can gently touch these traces — an object, a photograph, a recipe — and let them link the past with the present.
nostalgia.practice: Hold an object connected with what you miss, or recall it in every detail: its weight, its smell, its texture.

craving.text: A craving — a sharp "I want it right now" — can take you over completely, and that says nothing about weakness of character. New materialism suggests looking at it soberly and without reproach. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett writes about "thing-power": matter — food, chemical substances, objects — is not passive; it really does act on us. She devotes a whole chapter to how food affects mood and behaviour. From this point of view, a craving arises in an "assemblage" — made of the body, a substance, tiredness, advertising, a place, the time of day. This removes part of the shame: it isn't only "your weak will" that wants; the whole assemblage wants. But it also opens a possibility: you can change not your whole self but one element of the assemblage — the place, the time, what is near you. Sometimes that is enough for the wave to pass by.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, name three elements of the assemblage around it: where you are, what your body feels, what is near you. Try changing one — move to another room, step outside, message someone.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure. It is a loop that life has gradually been built into, and it is hard to get out of. New materialism helps us see why. Jane Bennett speaks of "distributive agency" — the idea that action rarely belongs to a single "I": it is spread across an assemblage of body, substances, habits, places, people, the economy. In addiction, this whole network is acting, and that is why willpower alone is often not enough. At the same time, Bennett doesn't remove the person from the picture: we are one of the nodes in the network and can influence how it is arranged. Donna Haraway adds the notion of "response-ability" — the capacity to respond, which grows not alone but in kinship with others. Seen this way, getting out of the loop is not a heroic battle with yourself but a gradual reassembling: new places, new rhythms, new connections.
addiction.practice: Draw the network around your loop: people, places, times, things. Mark one connection that could be strengthened a little — for example, a person you could talk to, or a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: A hangover is both pain in the body and morning anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. It's a hard morning, and you deserve gentleness. New materialism reminds us of a simple thing we often forget: we are made of matter. Jane Bennett writes that a human being is also in many ways "non-human": chemistry, microbes and minerals are at work in us, and they affect how we feel and think. Seen this way, part of the morning anxiety and the dark thoughts is the voice of a body that is recovering, not a final verdict on you. Your mood right now is shaped not only by what you did yesterday but also by what is happening in your body today. So you can treat it like weather: wait it out, take care of your body, and pass no verdicts on yourself until it changes.
hangover.practice: Tell yourself: "Right now my body is speaking in me too, not only my conscience." Do one simple act of care — a glass of water, fresh air, a warm shower.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid feeling: the world suddenly seems open, and you seem capable of anything. There's no need to hurry to "bring it down to earth". In The Enchantment of Modern Life, Jane Bennett argues with the familiar idea that the modern world is "disenchanted" and dull. She believes that moments of thrilling uplift and wonder are a real part of life, and they are valuable: such moments give energy, generosity, a desire to connect with the world. From the new materialist point of view, euphoria too is born in an assemblage — of body, light, people, music, events. This is useful to remember: the high is not only your personal "charge" but a fortunate convergence of circumstances that arrived and will, in its own time, change. You can rejoice in it fully — and notice what it was made of.
euphoria.practice: List what this high was made of: who was around, what was around you, what happened. Keep the list — it will help you recognise yourself on other days too.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high, a celebration or a success can be especially unpleasant: a moment ago everything was bright, and suddenly it has all gone dim. From the new materialist point of view, there is nothing mysterious about this, and certainly nothing shameful. Mood, as Jane Bennett writes, arises in an "assemblage" — made of the body, people, events, place. The party is over, people have gone home, the body is tired — the assemblage has come apart, and with it has gone the state it was holding. The drop is not proof that the high was "fake", and it is not the truth about your life. Donna Haraway calls on us to "stay with the trouble" — to flee neither into despair nor into hope of instant rescue, but to be in the present. You can stay with the drop in the same way: notice it, let your body recover, and little by little put together a new, calm assemblage of ordinary days.
crash.practice: Choose three simple elements for a "recovery assemblage" today — for example, warm food, a short walk, a conversation with someone — and put together at least one.

panic.text: A panic attack is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, and it seems something irreparable is about to happen. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes, though from the inside that is hard to believe. New materialism offers a particular support here — the matter around you. Jane Bennett writes that things are not passive: they act on us, and we are always connected to them. When a storm rages inside, the world of things stays close: the floor holds your weight, the chair supports your back, the cup cools your palm. Seen this way, you can lean not on a thought but on these material connections — literally. You are not alone with your body: you are part of an assemblage that includes the ground under your feet, the air, and objects ready to support you.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and feel how it holds you. Take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath, and name five objects around you — their colour or texture.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what's the point of it all", the thought of finitude, the sense of an abyss — is one of the heaviest experiences, and there is nothing shameful in it. New materialism doesn't promise a ready answer to the question of meaning, but it changes the picture itself. The physicist and philosopher Karen Barad writes that we don't stand "outside" the world, staring into a void: we are part of the world, entangled with it at every moment. Her key word is "intra-action": everything that exists arises within mutual relations, not on its own. Seen this way, the abyss is not the whole truth: you are already woven into a fabric where something responds to you. Donna Haraway calls us "mortal critters", entangled with others, and sees in this not a sentence but a ground for care and kinship. Meaning here is not a conclusion but a connection you can feel.
dread.practice: Name three threads that connect you to the world right now: a person, a living creature, a place. Stay for a minute with this feeling of being woven in.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out — the feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you are not where you should be — is very common in the age of feeds and stories. In her famous essay "Situated Knowledges", Donna Haraway criticises what she calls "the god trick" — the illusion that one can see everything at once from nowhere, from on high, without being in any particular place. A social media feed creates a similar illusion: it seems you are surveying all of life at once and missing what matters everywhere. But for Haraway every real view is "situated": it always comes from somewhere — from a particular body, place and history. Seen this way, there is no "right place"; there is your place — and it is no worse than others, simply the only one from which you can truly see and take part.
fomo.practice: Describe three details of your "here and now" that aren't in any feed: a smell, a sound, the light from the window.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are exhausting: the whole world seems to be asleep, and you are left alone with circling thoughts. New materialism helps lift part of the guilt from this. Sleep is not something you can order yourself to do by an effort of will. From Jane Bennett's point of view, one could say it arises in an assemblage: body, light, temperature, noise, a screen, the events of the day, the worries we brought with us. If sleep doesn't come, it isn't your personal failure but an assemblage that hasn't come together yet. You don't have to fight yourself; you can gently change what is around you: a little darker, a little cooler, a little quieter. Donna Haraway would remind you that the night is full of life: plants breathe, animals roam, somewhere other people are awake too. You are not alone in this night — you are part of its breathing.
sleepless.practice: Place a hand on your chest or belly and watch your breathing as you would watch a tide. You can silently list the living creatures that are also awake tonight.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds especially deeply because it comes from someone you trusted. This pain is legitimate. Donna Haraway writes a great deal about "response-ability" — the capacity to respond to another, to answer for a bond. She stresses that kinship is not a given but something we make, sustain and grow together. Seen this way, betrayal is a rupture of response-ability: the other stopped responding to your bond as it required. The responsibility for this rupture does not lie with you. And your own capacity to respond, to trust and to care has not gone anywhere — it is still yours. Haraway reminds us that webs of kinship can be wide: beyond one person there are friends, family, animals, places. You can lean on these threads while the wound heals.
betrayal.practice: Name three connections in your life that have stayed reliable — people, creatures or places. Stay a little with the thought of each.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonising: fear of loss, pain and anger are twisted together in it into a tight knot. From the new materialist point of view, one could say this feeling is understandable: we really are entangled with those we love — not metaphorically, but with our whole lives, habits, bodies. A threat to that bond is felt as a threat to part of ourselves. Donna Haraway suggests looking at relationships as "kinship", which is created and sustained by attention rather than owned by someone like a thing. A bond, in her view, lives in mutual response. Seen this way, you can listen to jealousy as a message about how much this bond matters to you — and notice that it cannot be held by force, but it can be sustained by attention and conversation. And one more thing: you are woven into more than one thread. Your life rests on a whole web of connections.
jealousy.practice: Write down: which thread of connection exactly am I afraid of losing? And what other threads are holding me right now?

resentment.text: An old grievance is a pain you carry with you, sometimes for years. It is legitimate: you really were treated unfairly. New materialism suggests looking at resentment as something almost material — it lives in the body: in tense shoulders, in thoughts that keep returning to one scene. Jane Bennett, with her idea of "distributive agency" — the thought that action is spread across many participants — shows that events are rarely created entirely by one person: circumstances, histories, pressures and webs of relations take part in them. Seen this way, one could say that this doesn't remove responsibility from the person who hurt you, but it lets you loosen a little the knot in which all the pain is tied to one figure. And Karen Barad writes that the past is never finally closed: its meaning keeps changing in the present. Resentment does not have to remain an unchanging burden.
resentment.practice: Notice where in your body the resentment lives — in your chest, your shoulders, your jaw. Place your palm there and take a few slow breaths out.

heartbreak.text: A breakup feels as if part of you has been torn out. From the new materialist point of view, this is no exaggeration. Donna Haraway says that we don't exist on our own but "become-with": in relationships we really do shape each other — habits, pet phrases, rhythms, even the way we move and eat. Karen Barad calls this "intra-action": the partners in a relation don't exist ready-made before it; they emerge within it. So when the bond breaks, you change too: it isn't only memory that hurts but the whole familiar order of life, bodily and everyday. This explains why the grief of a breakup is so physical. But what took shape in you during the relationship doesn't vanish — it remains yours. And the capacity to "become-with" remains too; in its own time it will find new connections — with people, places, pursuits.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one thing you learned in this relationship that will stay with you.

impostor.text: Impostor syndrome is the fear that you are about to be exposed and everyone will see that you are "not the real thing". Donna Haraway helps us look at this differently. In A Cyborg Manifesto she gives up the dream of a "pure", whole, natural identity: we are all hybrids, assembled from different histories, skills, accidents and other people's influences. Her idea of "situated knowledges" — all knowledge is partial and always looks from somewhere — means that no one sees or knows everything. Seen this way, the "real" expert who knows everything and depends on no one simply doesn't exist. Your feeling that "I'm put together from bits and pieces and there's a lot I don't know" is not an exposure but an honest description of how all knowledge works. Haraway prefers this honest incompleteness to the pose of an all-knowing goddess.
impostor.practice: Write down the "bits and pieces" your skill is made of: who you learned from, what you tried, where you made mistakes. This isn't a fake — it's your assemblage.

quote.text: I would rather be a cyborg than a goddess.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and a relentless inner critic are exhausting, and it's important to say straight away: the critic's verdict is not the truth about you. New materialism undermines its very logic in its own way. The critic speaks as if you were a separate, fully self-sufficient "I" that alone answers for everything that happens to it. But Jane Bennett and other new materialists show that we are assemblages: a body, a history, an environment, the people around us, the circumstances we grew up in. Everything you do and feel arises in the interaction of many forces. Rosi Braidotti, who is close to this current, speaks of an "affirmative" ethics: not negating the life in yourself but supporting its capacity to act and to rejoice. Seen this way, you deserve not judgement but care — the same care you would give any living creature.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine the critic saying these words about a plant or an animal you look after. What would you say to it instead of criticism? Write it down and address it to yourself.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling, when it seems that nothing depends on you. New materialism admits that in vast networks — the economy, the climate, politics — no single person really controls everything. But this thought has another side. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett recalls Darwin's studies of earthworms: tiny creatures, each almost invisible, create the fertile layer of soil over centuries. In a distributed network, action is made up of many small contributions. Donna Haraway warns both against "there's nothing to be done anymore" and against waiting for a miraculous rescue: both moods lead us away from the present. Seen this way, your small action is not nothing but part of a large assemblage. Being powerless before the whole doesn't cancel the fact that your contribution, like the work of those unnoticed creatures, also keeps the earth alive.
helplessness.practice: Name one very small action that is within your power today — and notice which people or creatures it connects you with.

procrastination.text: Procrastination is when a task hangs over you and you can't get started, and shame piles on top. New materialism suggests you stop seeing this as purely a problem of will. Jane Bennett writes that things have a power of their own: they dig in their heels, resist, attract or repel. A task is not only a thought in your head but a whole assemblage: the desk, the screen, a tired body, notifications, an unclear first step, the memory of past failures. If the assemblage doesn't come together into work, it isn't necessarily "laziness". Donna Haraway speaks of "sympoiesis" — "making-with": nothing is made alone. Seen this way, instead of pressuring yourself you can reassemble the circumstances: change your place, remove one distracting thing, invite someone to work alongside you. Sometimes what helps you start is not willpower but allies.
procrastination.practice: Find one thing in the assemblage around the task that you can change right now — move it, remove it, add it — and then take the smallest first step.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — emigration, a move, the ground slipping from under your feet — is a hard experience, and homesickness is legitimate. New materialism treats it with understanding, because it takes our connection to places seriously: the air, the landscape, the food, the sounds of your home street really were part of you. Rosi Braidotti, who has herself lived her life between several countries and languages, describes in Nomadic Subjects a "nomadic" identity — not as a loss of self but as a way of being yourself in motion, gathering connections in each new place. Donna Haraway speaks of "kinship" that is made, not only inherited. Seen this way, roots are not only what was left behind but also something you can put down anew: getting to know the trees on your street, the birds, the neighbours, the smells of a new place.
uprooted.practice: Choose one "resident" of your new place — a tree, a bird, a house along your way — and look at it closely, the way you would get to know a new acquaintance.

overload.text: Overload — a stream of news, messages, an endless feed — is draining, and it isn't a sign of your weakness. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett examines the great North American blackout of 2003: a vast power grid in which many elements — wires, stations, markets, flows of current — interacted in such a way that the system broke down. Bennett shows that networks have a life of their own that no one fully controls. From the new materialist point of view, one could say that your attention is also part of such a network: devices, apps and algorithms act on you, sometimes faster than you can decide anything. Tiredness from the stream is a signal of overload, like that of the power grid. Protecting yourself is not a matter of self-reproach but of reassembling: fewer incoming streams, more pauses and slow, tangible things.
overload.practice: Put your phone aside and for two minutes hold something slow and material — a stone, a cup, a plant. Notice its weight and temperature.

unreality.text: The feeling that the world or you yourself are somehow not real is a strange and unsettling experience, and it isn't easy to talk about. New materialism offers a gentle way back — through matter. For Karen Barad, reality is not a fixed backdrop that we observe from outside but something that constantly emerges in interactions: in touches, encounters, responses. In her essay "On Touching" she shows that even a simple touch is a complex event in which the "I" and the world meet. Seen this way, one could say that the sense of reality is not a given but something sustained by connection, and it can weaken when connections become few. Jane Bennett calls on us to notice things attentively — their weight, texture, springiness. Reality can be brought back little by little through the body: by touching, listening, feeling temperature.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object and describe five of its properties out loud: weight, temperature, texture, colour, the sound it makes.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, stars, the sea, music — is one of the deepest experiences, and new materialism values it especially. Jane Bennett considers "enchantment" — a feeling of being surprised and caught up by the world — an important force: in her view, it nourishes generosity and the wish to care. Interestingly, for her even something inconspicuous can be an occasion for awe. At the start of Vibrant Matter she describes how one day in Baltimore she saw, by a storm drain grate, a glove, a mat of pollen, a dead rat, a bottle cap and a stick — and suddenly felt the strange liveliness of these things. Seen this way, awe is the moment when the matter of the world opens itself to you in all its power. It doesn't need to be explained or used. You can simply stay in it and let it change the way you see.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, without taking a photo. Then find one small thing nearby and look at it just as attentively.

relief.text: Relief is when a load you have been carrying is suddenly lifted, and your body breathes out on its own. New materialism suggests taking this moment seriously, because relief is a very bodily event. Jane Bennett insists that we are material beings, and our states live not only in our thoughts: tension is held in the muscles, in the breath, in posture. Relief is the moment when this whole assemblage rearranges itself: the shoulders drop, the breath deepens, the world around becomes visible again. Seen this way, relief is not a trifle, nor a reason to go looking for a new worry right away. It is your body coming back to itself. You can live it fully and notice who and what helped it come: people, circumstances, chance, things.
relief.practice: Notice where in your body the relief is felt most strongly. Take a slow breath out and silently thank those — people, circumstances or things — who had a part in it.

calm.text: Calm is a rare and precious state: nothing is urgent, it's quiet inside. From the new materialist point of view, calm is not only an "inner" achievement but a fortunate assemblage: soft light, even breathing, a familiar mug, silence, a person or an animal nearby. Jane Bennett, who wrote a book about Henry Thoreau — the American thinker who spent two years in a cabin by Walden Pond — values his ability to notice the world around him attentively and unhurriedly. Such attention is calming in itself: you stop being only in your thoughts and find yourself among things and creatures. Donna Haraway would remind you that calm is almost always shared: plants breathe nearby, a cat sleeps, water flows. You can treasure it without analysing too much — simply noticing who and what is sharing it with you right now.
calm.practice: Name three things or creatures that are sharing this calm with you right now, and stay with them for another minute.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the moment when thoughts and images seem to arrive by themselves and you want to act. New materialism suggests understanding it almost literally: inspiration comes from outside. In Influx and Efflux, written in dialogue with Walt Whitman's poetry, Jane Bennett reflects on how the world constantly flows into us — through air, sounds, images, other people — and flows back out in our words and actions. Donna Haraway speaks of "sympoiesis" — "making-with": nothing is made alone; all creativity is shared with people, creatures and things. Seen this way, inspiration is not the exclusive merit of a lonely genius but a fortunate meeting of currents. You can rejoice in it and notice what exactly flowed into it — so that you can return to those sources again.
inspiration.practice: Write down what "flowed into" this inspiration: a conversation, a book, a walk, an image. And one line about what you want to "let out" of it into the world.

quote.text: It matters what stories make worlds, what worlds make stories.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — a small warm wave when something goes wrong for someone — is familiar to almost everyone, and it usually brings instant shame. On its own, this feeling says little about what kind of person you are. Rosi Braidotti, who is close to new materialism, follows Spinoza in distinguishing sad passions, which diminish our power to live, from joyful ones, which increase it. She proposes an "affirmative ethics" — not denying dark feelings but transforming them. Seen this way, schadenfreude is joy, but joy borrowed from someone else's failure: it rests on a picture of the world as a competition, where another's loss is your gain. If you notice this picture, you can ask what your own life is missing if it feeds itself this way. The answer usually speaks of your tiredness or hurt, not of malice.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, ask yourself: which need of my own just got some comfort? Write it down in one word.

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling that looks down from above, and it often arises as a defence: against disappointment, against powerlessness, against the fear of turning out to be similar. Having it is human. In When Species Meet, Donna Haraway draws attention to the word "respect": the Latin respicere means "to look back, to look again". For her, to respect is not to stop at the first glance but to notice the other again and again, their "significant otherness" — the ways they really are different, without being lesser for it. From Haraway's point of view, one could say that contempt is a gaze that has decided not to look again: the other is frozen in a single picture. You don't have to force yourself to love someone you despise. But you can notice that contempt hides the complexity of the world from you — and that behind it there is often pain of your own.
contempt.practice: Think of a person you feel contempt for and try to "look again": name one trait of theirs that doesn't fit your judgement.

disgust.text: Disgust is a very bodily feeling: the body recoils before you have time to think. It can be directed at a situation, at people, sometimes at yourself, and it doesn't make you a bad person. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett describes how she once saw some debris in a storm drain: a glove, a bottle cap, a stick, a dead rat. At first — the usual recoil. And then the things suddenly showed themselves as lively, strangely active participants in the world, and disgust mingled with wonder. Bennett doesn't ask us to love trash; she shows that the line between "clean" and "vile" is largely drawn by us. Seen this way, disgust is the body's signal about a boundary it wants to hold. It deserves respect. But sometimes you can make out something else behind it — vulnerability, fear, even curiosity.
disgust.practice: When you feel disgust, note where exactly in your body it lives, and ask: what boundary is it guarding right now?

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were treated unfairly, and you want the person who hurt you to feel pain too. This feeling doesn't make you cruel — it speaks of how deeply you were hurt. Jane Bennett suggests seeing action as "distributed": almost any event is produced by an assemblage of many participants — people, circumstances, tiredness, things, old histories. From Bennett's point of view, one could say that revenge rests on a simplification: as if all the harm were gathered in one person, and if you strike at them, the world will be set level. Bennett doesn't cancel responsibility, but she widens the picture. Then you can hear the wish for revenge as a demand for justice and protection — and ask what would truly restore your footing. The feeling remains yours; you don't have to act on it by causing harm.
revenge.practice: Finish the sentence: "If justice were restored, I would feel…" Listen to what this part of you wants.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — can be very strong, and then comes the shame: "how could I be so angry with them?" It is one of the most human of feelings, and it doesn't cancel love. Donna Haraway insists that kinship is not harmony but "trouble": a living, difficult, tangled bond in which collisions are inevitable. Jane Bennett adds that our state is produced by an assemblage: hunger, lack of sleep, noise, a long day, small things piling up. Seen this way, an evening outburst at someone you love is not a verdict on your relationship or the truth about you, but an event in which many things took part. This doesn't remove the wish to make things right, but it helps you do so without punishing yourself. Anger can show where you yourself are short of care.
anger_at_loved.practice: Recall the last time you snapped at someone close to you, and list what else was in that assemblage: tiredness, hunger, noise, hurry.

ambivalence.text: Loving a person and at the same time being unable to stand them is a heavy, tangled feeling, and it seems you must finally decide which of the two is true. Donna Haraway suggests not rushing to choose. In A Cyborg Manifesto she rejects the familiar binary divisions — nature or culture, body or mind, self or other — and values irony as the ability to hold incompatible things together. Seen this way, your mixed feelings are not a mistake and not a sign that the love is "fake". Someone close to you is not a simple object but a living tangle, and your bond with them is a tangle too: it holds tenderness, irritation and history. Both sides can be true at once. To admit this is to stop waging war on yourself.
ambivalence.practice: Write two sentences: "What I love in you is…" and "What I can't stand in you is…" — and leave them side by side without choosing.

quote.text: Irony is about contradictions that do not resolve into larger wholes, even dialectically, about the tension of holding incompatible things together because both or all are necessary and true.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, after someone's death, or after the end of a loved one's long illness often comes together with shame: "how can I feel relieved?" But relief and love get along perfectly well. New materialism reminds us that we are bodily beings. Long caregiving, worry, sleepless nights — this is tension that has lived for months in the muscles, the breath, sleep. When it goes, the body breathes out by itself, without asking permission. Karen Barad speaks of "entanglement": what is truly connected doesn't come untangled simply because circumstances have changed. Seen this way, your bond with the person doesn't vanish because things have become easier for you. Relief is not betrayal but a sign of how heavy the load was. You can allow yourself both.
guilty_relief.practice: Place your palm on your chest and tell yourself: "It has become easier for me, and I still love." Stay with this for a minute.

indifference.text: Sometimes something happens that "should" move you — someone else's grief, an important event — and inside it is quiet. And on top of the indifference comes anxiety: "is something wrong with me?" Donna Haraway speaks of "response-ability" — the capacity to respond. But for her every response is situated: it is born in a particular body, at a particular moment, with a particular store of strength. No one can respond to everything at once. Jane Bennett adds that the capacity to be enchanted and to feel compassion is not a permanent property of the soul but a state that depends on the assemblage: tiredness, overload, how much you have already been through. Seen this way, indifference is not proof of callousness but a sign that your capacity to respond is exhausted for now. Feelings often come back later, when there is room for them.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: what have I already responded to today and this week? Make a short list — it may explain the quiet inside.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and go somewhere no one knows you can be very strong. It is legitimate: this is often the voice of something that has long had no room. Jane Bennett sees life as an "assemblage" — made of people, places, things, rhythms, obligations. Some assemblages hold us up; others slowly drain us. Seen this way, the wish to run away is not weakness or a whim but a signal that your current assemblage has stopped holding you. Donna Haraway, speaking of the difficulties of our time, suggests "staying with the trouble" — throwing yourself neither into despair nor into a dream of instant rescue, but carefully working out what is happening. This doesn't mean leaving is not allowed. It means you can first understand which part of the assemblage exactly you want to be free of.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: "What I most want to run away from is…" — and name one specific part, not your whole life.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is "off limits" — an unavailable person, or the "wrong" one — often brings turmoil and shame, as if the feeling itself were already a wrongdoing. But attraction doesn't ask permission, and it says little about your decency. New materialism takes the force of attraction seriously. Jane Bennett writes about "thing-power" — the world's capacity to seize and draw us in — and Karen Barad says that desire and yearning belong to matter itself, not only to our "corrupt" will. Seen this way, attraction is the force of an encounter passing through you, not an order you are obliged to carry out or suppress. You can approach it with curiosity: what exactly about this person makes you feel so alive? Often the answer says more about your own life than about them.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down in a word or two what quality in this person draws you so strongly. Then ask: where else in my life is this quality missing?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgement — stiffness, a burning face, the wish to become invisible — is very draining, and you are not alone in it. Karen Barad speaks of "intra-action": the participants in an encounter don't exist as ready-made, separate figures who then collide — they take shape within the interaction itself. Seen this way, one could say that in a conversation there is no fixed judge and no fixed defendant: you are not being "assessed" as a finished thing; together with others you create a situation in which they too are nervous and they too don't know things. And Jane Bennett would remind you that the body is a full participant: a pounding heart and a trembling voice are not "weakness of character" but the body's own reaction. It can be met gently, not with reproach.
social_anxiety.practice: Next time, before a meeting, note: "The other person is feeling something right now too." And take one slow breath out.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty — not knowing what will happen — is draining: the mind tries again and again to calculate everything in advance. Karen Barad, a physicist and philosopher, follows Niels Bohr in showing that indeterminacy is not simply a shortfall in our knowledge. For her it is a feature of reality itself: much is not settled in advance but becomes determinate only in the course of interactions. In her essay "Situated Knowledges", Donna Haraway adds that it is impossible to see everything at once from above — all knowledge is partial and made from somewhere. Seen this way, you don't have to know the future in order to act honestly. Uncertainty is not your personal failure at forecasting but part of how the world is made. There is less threat in it if you remember: not yet decided also means still open.
uncertainty.practice: Write: "I don't know what will happen with…, but right now I know that…" — and complete the second part with one fact about the present.

quote.text: Only partial perspective promises objective vision.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — is one of the most drawn-out states: time stretches, and it's hard to get on with anything else. Jane Bennett speaks of "distributive agency": almost any outcome is produced by many participants at once — people, machines, procedures, bodies, weather. Seen this way, while you wait, things are not standing still: somewhere lab analysers are running, letters are being read, a decision is taking shape. It's just that this part of the assemblage isn't in your hands right now. Donna Haraway loves images of slow processes — growth, ripening, compost — in which much happens invisibly. Waiting is agonising partly because it seems to us that everything depends on our straining. Acknowledging that others are acting now is not passivity but an honest picture, in which you can loosen your grip a little.
waiting.practice: Name who or what is "working" right now on what you are waiting for. Then choose one small task that depends only on you.

regret.text: Regret over something done or not done can come back again and again: "if only I had…" This feeling speaks of what mattered to you. Reflecting on quantum experiments, Karen Barad offers an unexpected thought: the past is not closed once and for all. She stresses that its traces are not erased — what was done stays done. But what the past turns out to be keeps taking shape in new interactions: its meaning, consequences and connections are not yet complete. From Barad's point of view, one could say that regret is not only longing for what cannot be brought back but also taking part in what the past will become. You can't replay that moment, but you can influence what grows out of it — including through how you treat it now.
regret.practice: Write down one regret, and beneath it: "What could grow out of this now is…" — and add one small possibility.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person — their voice, their smell, the way they laugh — can be almost physical. And that is no exaggeration. New materialism takes seriously the fact that feelings live in matter: in the body, in things, in places. Karen Barad speaks of "entanglement" — connections that don't disappear when the participants part. Seen this way, your longing is not weakness and not being "stuck" but living evidence of how entangled you are with this person: your habits, pet phrases, even gestures carry their trace. Longing reminds you of a bond that keeps acting even at a distance. You don't have to drive it away; you can cherish it as a sign that the meeting was real.
longing.practice: Find one object near you connected with this person, or recall a gesture of theirs that has passed on to you. Stay with it for a minute.

quote.text: Matter feels, converses, suffers, desires, yearns and remembers.
quote.author: Karen Barad
quote.source: interview in New Materialism: Interviews & Cartographies (2012)

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — grim news, wars, injustice — can overwhelm you so much that it's hard to live your own life. This pain is legitimate: it speaks of your connection with others. Rosi Braidotti, who is close to new materialism, puts it this way: we are all in this together, but we are not one and the same. Suffering is unequally distributed, and your pain is a response to someone else's, not a copy of it. Braidotti proposes an "affirmative ethics" — neither denying pain nor drowning in it, but transforming it into a capacity to act together with others. Donna Haraway would add that "staying with the trouble" means not turning away, but also not demanding that you carry the whole world alone. Your part of the response can be small and still be real.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small act of response that fits your strength today — to help, to support, to talk. And one act of caring for yourself.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds painfully: it seems a verdict has been passed on you — "you don't fit". This pain is real. Karen Barad offers the notion of an "agential cut": the boundaries between "ours" and "theirs", "inside" and "outside" are not given in advance but are drawn in specific interactions — here and now, under these conditions. Seen this way, one could say that rejection is one such cut, made in one situation, by one person or group. It is real and painful, but it is not the final truth about your essence. In other encounters, under other conditions, the boundary will fall differently. New materialism in general doubts that a person has an unchanging essence that anyone could definitively judge. You are an ongoing process, and a single "no" doesn't bring it to an end.
rejection.practice: Write: "In this situation, with these people, the boundary fell like this." Then name one place or person where it falls differently.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be sharp and clinging: every silence from someone close seems like the beginning of the end. This fear is understandable — behind it is the wish to be in a secure bond. Donna Haraway loves the image of string figures — the children's game in which a pattern passes from hand to hand: one holds, another picks it up, and the figure lives as long as it is passed on. For her, this is how the bonds between living beings work too — through many hands. Seen this way, the fear of abandonment is especially strong when your whole figure is held by a single pair of hands. This doesn't mean the most important person matters less. But you can also notice the other threads — friends, places, pursuits, animals — that also hold the pattern of your life. The more of them there are, the less each pause feels like a break.
abandonment.practice: Draw yourself as a dot and draw lines to everyone and everything that holds you right now — people, places, pursuits. Look at the drawing.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts in a particular way: the feeling is enormous, and there is no answer. And the pain is often joined by the question "what's wrong with me?" In The Companion Species Manifesto, Donna Haraway speaks of "significant otherness": the other is not a mirror of our desires but a truly different being with their own life, rhythm and choices. To love is to meet this otherness, including the possibility that it may not answer us in kind. Seen this way, unrequitedness is not a verdict on your worth but an encounter with the other's freedom. And new materialism would add: your feeling doesn't become any less real because of this. It really acts in you, changes you, opens you. You can grieve for what didn't happen and at the same time respect the fact that you are capable of loving like this.
unrequited.practice: Write: "My love has taught me…" — and complete it with one discovery about yourself that it brought.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: it is as if you have been pushed lower than you are. This pain is legitimate, and the blame for the humiliation does not lie with you. In A Cyborg Manifesto, Donna Haraway shows that the familiar pairs of "higher and lower" — mind and body, human and animal, culture and nature — have served a logic of domination: someone is always placed above and someone below. New materialism tries to flatten this ladder: instead of a hierarchy, a network in which each participant has their own weight and their own force. Seen this way, humiliation is an attempt to force you onto the bottom rung of a ladder that doesn't really exist in the world. It wounds, but it doesn't determine your place. Your dignity doesn't depend on whoever tried to take it away.
humiliation.practice: Say to yourself out loud, or write: "What was done to me is about them and the situation, not about my worth."

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background: a glance in the mirror, comparisons, a wish to hide. It's understandable — from childhood we are taught to look at the body as a shop window. New materialism offers a different view. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett reminds us that the body is a community: billions of bacteria live in it, and countless processes you never think about are at work. In A Cyborg Manifesto, Donna Haraway gives up the dream of a "pure", "natural", ideal body: we are all hybrids. Seen this way, the body is not a picture to be rated but a living assemblage that every day breathes, digests, repairs itself and carries you through the world. You don't have to love every feature of it, and you can still respect what it does.
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body did for you today — not how it looks, but what it did: breathed, walked, held, felt.

illness.text: Illness, when the body lets you down, is a hard experience: it hurts, it's frightening, and often a grudge against your own body appears. These feelings are legitimate. In her essay on "the biopolitics of postmodern bodies", Donna Haraway examined how often the body and immunity are spoken of in the language of war: "fighting", "enemies", "defeat". Such language quietly turns the ill person into a loser. From the new materialist point of view, the body is not a machine commanded by the will and not a battlefield, but a living assemblage of many participants, not all of whom obey us. Jane Bennett reminds us that matter has its own power. Illness is not your fault and not a betrayal by your body, but an event that is happening to you and in you. You can treat your body as an ally in a difficult time, not as a culprit.
illness.practice: Place your palm on the part of your body that is struggling right now and silently say: "We're going through this together."

pride.text: Pride in something you've done is a good, deserved feeling; there's no need to hide it. New materialism is sometimes understood as dissolving personal merit: if assemblages do the acting, there's nothing to be proud of. But Jane Bennett is saying something else. For her, action is distributed — people, tools and circumstances take part in it — and your role in this assemblage is entirely real. You were the node where everything came together; you chose, persisted, invested yourself. Acknowledging the other participants doesn't take away your contribution; it makes your pride calmer and warmer: there is less rivalry in it and more joy that things worked out. Seen this way, you can be proud with all your heart and at the same time thank those who helped. One doesn't get in the way of the other.
pride.practice: Name what exactly you are proud of, and finish the sentence: "My contribution was that I…" And then name one helper — a person or a thing.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a quiet, slightly sad and yet warm state, like an autumn evening. It doesn't need fixing. New materialism invites you to see in it not only an "inner" mood but an encounter with the world. Jane Bennett writes that mood is made up of many participants: light, weather, sounds, smells, memories, the body. Autumn light, rain outside the window, an old song really do take part in your melancholy — it is made together with them. Bennett also values quiet forms of enchantment: not rapture, but an attentive, slightly sad stillness before the fragility of things. Seen this way, melancholy is a way of feeling especially finely that everything passes and is therefore precious. You can simply stay in it, as in good weather.
melancholy.practice: Note what is taking part in your mood right now: light, sound, weather, a memory. Name them and stay with them.
